newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges Congress to wrap up budget promptly.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges Congress to wrap up budget promptly.

text.p: President Bill Clinton urged Congress on Saturday to act promptly on wrapping up the broad outlines of the balanced budget plan when the House and Senate return next week after a 10-day recess.

As lawmakers departed May 23, loose ends were left to be tied up in the five-year budget agreement, which passed both houses with strong bipartisan support. Minor differences in their separate versions remained to be reconciled.
"When Congress gets back to work, it's time to finish the job of enacting the broad outlines of the budget plan," Clinton said in his weekly radio address.
Then, the president said, the task of filling in the details and writing the budget and its tax cut into law could begin.
"The American people deserve a tax cut and they need a balanced budget. We can give them both," he declared.
Clinton laid out his goals for a tax cut, saying it must help working families, open the doors of college to every American and never throw the budget out of balance.

"We cannot put our prosperity at risk through time-bomb tax cuts that explode the deficit in five or 10 or 20 years," he said. "We must continue with discipline. We tried it the other way before and it failed."

The balanced budget agreement, reached after months of meetings between Republican leaders in Congress and White House negotiators, slows the growth of government spending for the next five years. It cuts Medicare for the elderly by $115 billion and brings the deficit down to zero by 2002 from this year's forecast level of $67 billion.
It also provides a net $85 bilion tax cut, which Republicans assured the White House would largely benefit families with children and those in which students were seeking post-secondary education.
"The tax cuts must be consistent with a balanced budget and must not be written in such a way that they reopen the deficit and bust the budget in years to come," Clinton said.
"This was absolutely key when we reached a budget agreement and I will continue to insist upon it as we write the agreement into law," he added.

In his radio address, which came a day after the government released figures showing the economy grew at its fastest pace in nine years as 1997 opened, Clinton bragged that his policies had led to the healthiest U.S. economy in a generation.
"Today our confidence has returned and our economy leads the world. All this didn't just happen," he said.

Noting that four years ago, high unemployment, a lack of new jobs, stagnant wages and exploding budget deficits plagued the country, Clinton said: "I took office determined to replace trickle-down economics with invest-and-grow economics."

"Just look at the results ... inflation is at a 30-year low, business investment, a 30-year high. Each year we've had a record number of new businesses started. Wages are rising ... Our economy is the healthiest in a generation," he said.
